subject: english
title: Work & office
description: Meeting language, deadlines and status updates — the vocabulary of a working day.

content.title: Why this set
content.body: Most professional English is a small, repeated vocabulary: scheduling, reporting status, flagging risk, asking for time. Knowing forty phrases well beats knowing four hundred vaguely.

content.title: Collocations, not single words
content.body: Learn the whole phrase: meet a deadline, raise a concern, follow up on an email, take minutes, be on annual leave. The verb is the part that is hard to guess.

content.title: Good practice
content.body: "I will revert to you" is common in some regions but reads oddly to most native speakers — "I'll get back to you" is the safe choice.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: We need to ___ the deadline on Friday.
exercises.explanation: The collocation is meet a deadline. You can also miss or extend one, but never reach or catch one.

exercises.question: Which phrase proposes moving a meeting to a later date?

answers.text: Shall we push the meeting up to Thursday?
Shall we push the meeting back to Thursday?
Shall we push out of the meeting on Thursday?
Shall we push away the meeting to Thursday?

exercises.explanation: push back means delay; push up (or bring forward) means make earlier.

exercises.question: Translate the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Jestem w trakcie — skończę do czwartku.

answers.text: It's in progress — I'll have it done since Thursday.
It's on progress — I'll have it done until Thursday.
I am during it — I finish to Thursday.
It's in progress — I'll have it done by Thursday.

exercises.explanation: in progress, and by Thursday for a deadline. until Thursday would mean the work continues up to that point.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.back: wrócić do sprawy / dopytać po czasie
exercises.explanation: I'll follow up on that email tomorrow. The preposition on is not optional.

exercises.question: "I'm on annual leave next week" means you are away on holiday.
exercises.explanation: annual leave is the formal British term for paid holiday; PTO is the common American equivalent.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: I'd like to ___ a concern about the timeline.
exercises.explanation: raise a concern / raise an issue / raise a ticket. It is the standard verb for putting something on the table.

exercises.question: Why do native speakers write "Could you possibly send it today?" rather than "Send it today"?

answers.text: Indirect forms signal politeness; a bare imperative reads as an order
The longer form is more precise about the deadline
There is no difference in tone
The imperative is grammatically incorrect in email

exercises.explanation: English carries politeness through indirectness and modals. Polish often carries it through the word for please instead, which is why direct translations can sound blunt.

exercises.question: What are "minutes" in a meeting context?

answers.text: The written record of what was discussed and decided

exercises.explanation: You take minutes during a meeting and circulate them afterwards. The agenda is what you plan to cover.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.back: mam urwanie głowy / jestem zawalony robotą
exercises.explanation: Informal but very common. "I'm at capacity" is the neutral register, "I have a lot on" the British understatement.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Just a gentle ___ about the access request from Monday.
exercises.explanation: "A gentle reminder" is the standard polite chaser. Remind is the verb: may I remind you.

exercises.question: Which reply declines most professionally?

answers.text: I won't be able to join, but could you share the notes afterwards?

exercises.explanation: A reason plus an alternative is the expected shape. A bare negative reads as abrupt in English even when it is perfectly polite in Polish.

exercises.question: Translate the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Jestem zablokowany — czekam na dostęp do środowiska.

answers.text: I am blocked — I wait for the environment access.
I am on block — waiting to environment access.
I am blocking — I am waiting on the environment access.
I'm blocked — I'm waiting for access to the environment.

exercises.explanation: "I'm blocked" is the standard stand-up phrase, and waiting takes for. "Waiting on" is American and more common about people than things.

exercises.question: "Please find attached the report" is acceptable but dated; "I've attached the report" reads more naturally today.
exercises.explanation: Both are understood. Modern business English prefers the direct active form.

exercises.question: In meeting notes, what does "AI: Anna to confirm scope by Friday" mean?

answers.text: Action item — a task with an owner and a deadline

exercises.explanation: Minutes usually pair AI (action item) with an owner and a date. TBC means to be confirmed; TBD, to be decided.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.explanation: I'll loop in the platform team. The opposite is to take someone off the thread.
